identification.summary: Microsoft describes Storm-1865 as a cluster of activity conducting phishing campaigns that lead to payment data theft and fraudulent charges [S1]. It is a Microsoft 'group in development' designation, not a named nation-state actor [S3]. Microsoft reported in March 2025 that the cluster impersonated Booking.com to target hospitality staff with ClickFix lures [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft says the campaigns have been ongoing with increased volume since at least early 2023 [S1]. The Booking.com ClickFix activity began in December 2024 and was still ongoing as of February 2025 [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Storm-1865 (group in development); the Microsoft mapping lists no other vendor names [S3]. No MITRE ATT&CK group was identified in the sources gathered. Overlap with other clusters that use ClickFix or the same commodity malware is not established in the cited sources.

attribution.confidence: Microsoft characterizes the activity as a cluster conducting phishing for payment data theft and fraudulent charges, and does not state a sponsor [S1]. No government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: Microsoft Threat Intelligence reporting (March 2025) [S1], with trade-press coverage repeating Microsoft's findings [S2].

objectives: Financial fraud and theft: payloads steal financial data and credentials for use in fraudulent activity, which Microsoft calls a hallmark of Storm-1865 activity [S1].

sectors: Hospitality (hotels, and individuals likely to work with Booking.com) [S1]
regions: Northern, Southern, Eastern and Western Europe [S1]
targeting.notes: Microsoft says Storm-1865 identifies hospitality organizations and then targets individuals likely to work with Booking.com [S1]. Earlier targeting shifted from hotel guests (2023) to e-commerce buyers (2024) to hospitality staff (2024-2025) [S1].

capabilities.summary: Phishing emails impersonating Booking.com (themes: negative guest reviews, prospective guest requests, promotion opportunities, account verification) carry a link or a PDF containing a link [S1]. The link leads to a fake CAPTCHA over a page mimicking Booking.com; the ClickFix step tells the victim to open the Windows Run dialog and paste a command the page placed on the clipboard, which uses mshta.exe to fetch and run code [S1]. Payloads observed include XWorm, Lumma Stealer, VenomRAT, AsyncRAT, Danabot and NetSupport RAT, delivered as PowerShell, JavaScript and PE content [S1]. Messages were sent through vendor platforms and email services such as Gmail or iCloud Mail [S1]. Capability appears to rely on commodity malware and social engineering rather than exploits [S1].

campaigns.name: Booking.com guest phishing
campaigns.summary: Microsoft says Storm-1865 targeted Booking.com hotel guests with similar social engineering and malware.

campaigns.name: E-commerce buyer phishing
campaigns.summary: Phishing messages aimed at e-commerce platform buyers led to fraudulent payment webpages.

campaigns.name: Booking.com ClickFix campaign against hospitality
campaigns.summary: Fake Booking.com emails and a fake CAPTCHA/ClickFix page delivered XWorm, Lumma Stealer, VenomRAT, AsyncRAT, Danabot and NetSupport RAT to hospitality staff in North America, Oceania, South and Southeast Asia and Europe; ongoing as of February 2025.

campaigns.name: Microsoft public reporting
campaigns.summary: Microsoft published its analysis and IOCs (C2 IPs for XWorm, Danabot, Lumma Stealer and AsyncRAT, plus Danabot hashes).

diamond.adversary: Unattributed financially motivated phishing cluster tracked by Microsoft [S1][S3].
diamond.capability: Booking.com-themed phishing, fake CAPTCHA/ClickFix, mshta.exe execution, commodity RATs and infostealers [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Phishing pages mimicking Booking.com; email sent via vendor platforms and Gmail/iCloud Mail; malware C2 IP addresses published by Microsoft [S1].
diamond.victim: Hospitality organizations and staff who work with Booking.com; earlier hotel guests and e-commerce buyers [S1].
diamond.socioPolitical: Financial fraud and theft; no political motive stated [S1].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints where users can open the Run dialog and execute mshta.exe; email and PDF delivery channels [S1].

gaps: No sponsor, nationality or operator identity is stated in the sources gathered; Microsoft describes only a cluster [S1].
No activity after the March 2025 report was found in searches; current status is unknown.
Exact 2023 and 2024 campaign details and scale are only summarized by Microsoft; no primary detail was found [S1].
Relationship to other ClickFix or Booking.com-themed phishing clusters from other vendors is not established.
Microsoft's full IOC list was not independently verified; the Microsoft page was read via fetch summary only.
No MITRE ATT&CK group entry was identified, so technique mapping is unavailable.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: This is a criminal, not state, cluster; relevance to DoD is indirect, through hospitality and travel booking used by personnel on official or personal travel and through commodity RATs that can persist on any Windows endpoint [S1]. STEP 2: Environment: Windows users who can run mshta.exe and the Run dialog, and who handle booking-platform email [S1]. STEP 3: Template is brand-impersonation email, fake CAPTCHA/ClickFix, mshta.exe, then a stealer or RAT such as Lumma, XWorm or NetSupport [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued payment-data and credential theft from hospitality targets [S1]. MDCOA is that the same ClickFix chain is reused against other brands or sectors, and RAT access is resold or reused for later intrusion; this is not supported by the cited sources beyond the observed shift in targets across years [S1]. Candidate indicators: mshta.exe launched from the Run dialog, clipboard-pasted commands, and Microsoft-published C2 IPs [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track ClickFix-style user-execution lures as an end-user risk, particularly for travel-related email [S1]. (2) Authorities: handling of personal travel accounts and commercial email is outside most mission networks; response likely stays with local network defense and reporting through normal channels. (3) Mission assurance: endpoint controls Microsoft recommends (attack surface reduction rules, SmartScreen, network protection, phishing-resistant MFA) reduce exposure [S1]. (4) Coordination: share the Microsoft IOCs with network defenders and train users not to paste clipboard commands into the Run dialog [S1].
